query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Grain-boundary diffusion of Al and Cr in the fcc matrix drives the formation of a thin, protective oxide layer that limits further degradation at elevated temperatures. Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation along the grain boundaries produces an adherent alumina/chromia scale which preserves the alloy’s bulk mechanical integrity, whereas under reducing conditions, the absence or partial reduction of this scale leads to increased intergranular degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix exhibiting balanced strength and fatigue performance
generation.intervention: subject samples to controlled elevated-temperature exposure in either oxidizing (oxygen-rich) or reducing (hydrogen-rich) atmospheres
generation.conditions: temperatures sufficiently high to activate grain-boundary diffusion (e.g., 700-900 °C) for durations long enough to develop measurable oxide scales, with atmospheric conditions well-controlled to ensure either net oxidizing or reducing environments
generation.structural_mediator: grain-boundary regions where Al and Cr enrichment allow local oxidation, forming a coherent, thin alumina/chromia scale
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing atmospheres, Al and Cr diffuse along grain boundaries to form a thin, adherent oxide scale that acts as a barrier against further oxidation, maintaining mechanical integrity. Under reducing conditions, the diminished presence or partial reduction of this passivating oxide layer leads to accelerated oxidation at exposed sites, resulting in intergranular degradation which may compromise the high-performance mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting-state alloy, samples exposed in oxidizing environments will exhibit a stable, thin oxide scale at grain boundaries with minimal loss in mechanical integrity; samples in reducing atmospheres will show less-developed or disrupted oxide scales and increased evidence of intergranular degradation, which could correlate with reduced mechanical performance over time.
generation.baseline: properties and oxidation behavior of the as-manufactured alloy under inert or neutral conditions without significant external oxidizing or reducing driving forces
generation.boundary: the hypothesis is expected to hold at elevated temperatures (around 700-900 °C) over exposure durations sufficient to manifest grain-boundary oxidation effects; deviations outside this temperature range or significantly longer exposure times (leading to phase readjustments) may introduce additional degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thickness and stability of the protective oxide scale, as well as the quantitative contribution of grain-boundary versus bulk oxidation processes, remain uncertain. Additionally, the interactions of other elements present (e.g., Ti, Co, Fe, Ni) might modulate the oxidation kinetics in ways not completely accounted for by this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of identical alloy samples. Expose one set to an oxidizing atmosphere and another set to a reducing atmosphere at 750 °C for durations ranging from 50 to 200 hours. Characterize the near-surface and grain boundary regions using high-resolution electron microscopy and energy dispersive spectroscopy to map oxide layer formation and assess continuity. Additionally, perform mechanical tests (e.g., fatigue or tensile) post-exposure to correlate microstructural changes with performance degradation.
measurements: Thickness and uniformity of the oxide scale along grain boundaries (using TEM/SEM imaging and EDS mapping)
Phase identification of the oxide scales (using XRD or Raman spectroscopy)
Mechanical performance metrics (fatigue strength, tensile strength) before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under oxidizing conditions, no coherent or thin protective oxide scale is observed along grain boundaries, or if the alloy’s mechanical integrity degrades more rapidly than under reducing conditions despite the presence of the scale, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary diffusion of Al and Cr forms a passivating protective oxide scale would be falsified. Similarly, if reducing atmospheres show evidence of the same protective scale development as oxidizing conditions, the proposed mechanism is contradicted.
